lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on India’s missing factories
lead.head: Services sprint, factories stall

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 104

body: Indian man­u­fac­tur­ing is bro­ken, Ajay Shah de­clared, and he brought the num­bers to prove it. For 30 years its share of GDP has been stuck be­tween 15 and 20 per cent; in the mid­dle stage of de­vel­op­ment, coun­tries reach 40 to 50 per cent.
Its share of jobs is small and not ris­ing. The ex­port fig­ures are starker still[[x2]].
Over a decade, ser­vices ex­ports grew from $151 bil­lion to $341 bil­lion, a rise of 126 per cent. Goods ex­ports grew from $319 bil­lion to $442 bil­lion, only 38 per cent in nom­i­nal dol­lars.
Allow for American in­fla­tion, Shah said, and goods ex­ports grew at “about zero point five per­cent per year com­pounded ex­pressed in real USD, which is abysmal”. {104-C01}
The episode, the first of two[[x1]], grew out of Episode 419 of *The Seen and the Unseen*, Amit Varma’s con­ver­sa­tion with Sudhir Sarnobat and Naren Shenoy about the tra­vails of Indian busi­ness.
## Why the of­fice won

Why did ser­vices take off while fac­to­ries stalled? Varma’s short an­swer was that IT ser­vices were “rel­a­tively new for the Indian state. So it kind of got blind­sided by it.” Manufacturing had to carry decades of op­pres­sive reg­u­la­tion. {104-C02}

Shah gave the long an­swer: eight ways in which a fac­tory dif­fers from an of­fice. A fac­tory is vis­i­ble, so goons, neigh­bours and in­spec­tors all come call­ing. It needs sup­pli­ers close by, while ser­vices con­nect over fibre.
It must buy land and ma­chines and carry work­ing cap­i­tal. It moves goods, not elec­trons, and pays back over five to seven years rather than one or two.
Above all, it needs what Shah called “a cathe­dral of com­plex­ity”: a web of con­tracts that courts en­force quickly, so that sup­pli­ers de­liver on time.
## A his­tory of mis­takes
Varma sup­plied the his­tory. In 1750, he said, India made about 20 to 25 per cent of the world’s man­u­fac­tur­ing out­put, all of it ar­ti­sanal. By 1900 the share was 2 per cent.

Colonialism took part of the blame, but the big­ger cause, he ar­gued, was tech­no­log­i­cal ob­so­les­cence: “It just so hap­pens that we got un­lucky and in­dus­tri­alised a lit­tle later.” {104-S04}

After Independence the state made things worse. Jawaharlal Nehru’s mis­takes, im­port sub­sti­tu­tion and the be­lief that com­pe­ti­tion is waste­ful, fol­lowed the fash­ion of the times. What came after 1965 Varma called un­for­giv­able: India knew it was on the wrong track and went deeper. {104-C07}
The 1970s, when cheap labour could have made India a man­u­fac­tur­ing su­per­power, were lost.
## Twelve prob­lems, two gov­ern­ments

Shah then listed twelve prob­lems that hold man­u­fac­tur­ing back today: labour law and min­i­mum wages, land, the lo­ca­tion of work­ers, elec­tric­ity, trade bar­ri­ers, fi­nance, a state sus­pi­cious of the world, hos­til­ity to size, slow courts, un­re­funded taxes on ex­ports and a short­age of skilled peo­ple.
Infrastructure made the list too, but Shah no longer thinks it is the bind­ing con­straint.
Five of the twelve, he said, be­long to the union gov­ern­ment and seven to the states. “Each state is a mas­ter of its own des­tiny on seven out of the twelve things.” {104-C18}
Varma said he would watch the episode “again and again and again”, and might ask their ed­i­tor for a ver­sion with­out him­self in it.
Next week, the hosts promised, they would ask whether a coun­try can have a growth strat­egy in which man­u­fac­tur­ing is not of essence.

second.label: Services v manufacturing
second.head: A factory can’t hide
second.deck: Ajay Shah on why being visible is a liability for India’s factories

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on factories as sitting ducks

body: A fac­tory is big and bulky, and ev­ery­one can see it. Ajay Shah bor­rowed a word for this from James C. Scott’s *Seeing Like a State*: fac­to­ries are leg­i­ble[[x3]].

Once one goes up, local peo­ple ask it to fund a puja or build a school. Local goons de­mand money be­fore its trucks can pass. Every imag­in­able in­spec­tor shows up to ex­tort. Factories, Shah said, are sit­ting ducks. {104-C03}

A ser­vices firm sits on one floor of an in­nocu­ous of­fice build­ing, among many firms, with no sin­gle con­cen­trated owner. That, Shah said, makes ser­vices “a lit­tle more hid­den, it’s a lit­tle gen­teel”. {#genteel}

quote.text: All the prob­lems of ex­tor­tion and ex­pro­pri­a­tion by pri­vate per­sons and by state per­son­nel af­flict fac­to­ries more.

third.head: A tale of two Bengals

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the minimum wage

body: Ajay Shah of­fered what he called a North Korea-South Korea com­par­i­son: “a com­mu­nist coun­try called West Bengal, where the min­i­mum wage is 13,000 ru­pees”, and “a cap­i­tal­ist coun­try called East Bengal”, where he thought it was seven or eight thou­sand. {104-J06}

East Bengal built the amaz­ingly suc­cess­ful gar­ment ex­port in­dus­try[[x4]]. In India, Shah said, high min­i­mum wages leave only cap­i­tal-intensive gar­ment fac­to­ries vi­able, in a coun­try with mass poverty.
Amit Varma ex­plained why. If a worker’s labour is worth 8,000 ru­pees, a 13,000-rupee floor does not raise his pay. It makes his job il­le­gal[[x5]], and he earns “a big fat zero”. {104-C09}
Shah called it the state using “its mo­nop­oly of vi­o­lence” to stop a vol­un­tary deal be­tween con­sent­ing adults.

p2.deck: Ajay Shah’s diagnosis and Amit Varma’s history of how India’s state hobbled its factories, chapter by chapter

quote.text: There is a se­ri­ous cri­sis with man­u­fac­tur­ing in India.

box.title: Where the episode began
box.text: Ajay Shah called Episode 419 of *The Seen and the Unseen*, with Sudhir Sarnobat and Naren Shenoy[[x9]], one of its best. Four and a half hours long, it does the “ex­pen­sive, dif­fi­cult field work” re­searchers would oth­er­wise have to do. {#fieldwork}

sections.label: The hard facts
sections.head: Stuck at twenty per cent
sections.caption: the hard numbers
body: Ajay Shah set out to prove that Indian man­u­fac­tur­ing is bro­ken, with two qual­i­ta­tive claims and one set of hard num­bers.
The first claim: when GDP grows fast, manufacturing’s share should rise a lot. In India it has been stuck be­tween 15 and 20 per cent for 30 years. “20% of GDP ain’t much,” he said.
The sec­ond: manufacturing’s share of em­ploy­ment should rise with growth. It has no mean­ing­ful pres­ence in over­all em­ploy­ment, and it is not going up.
Amit Varma asked what a healthy fig­ure would be. In rich OECD economies the share de­clines again, Shah said, but there is a mid­dle zone where it goes up to 40 to 50 per cent of GDP.
## The ex­port test

The stark­est ev­i­dence was in ex­ports[[x10]]. Services ex­ports grew from $151 bil­lion to $341 bil­lion in a decade, a gain of 126 per cent. “That hap­pened to my weight, but con­tinue,” Varma said. {104-J04}
Goods ex­ports grew from $319 bil­lion to $442 bil­lion, 38 per cent in nom­i­nal dol­lars. American in­fla­tion in the decade was al­most 3 per cent, Shah noted, not the 2 per cent tar­get.
That leaves real growth of about half a per cent a year, “which is abysmal”. {104-C01}
~ “It be­hoves all of us,” Shah said, “to think about what is wrong and what should be done about it.”

quote.text: There is a se­ri­ous cri­sis with man­u­fac­tur­ing in India.

sections.label: Factory v office
sections.head: Electrons travel light
sections.caption: why factories differ from offices
body: Ajay Shah counted eight ways in which a man­u­fac­tur­ing prob­lem dif­fers from a ser­vices prob­lem. The first, that fac­to­ries are vis­i­ble and so at­tract ex­tor­tion, he called leg­i­bil­ity.

The sec­ond is link­ages. Factories thrive among spe­cialised sup­pli­ers close by, but in India some­thing trips up a few of them. “One fel­low will go down with a labour law, one fel­low will go down with some banks and cred­i­tors,” he said. Services con­nect over fibre-optic ca­bles[[x11]] and do not care where any­one sits. {104-C04}

Then cap­i­tal: a ser­vices firm rents its floor and its com­put­ing, while a fac­tory buys land and ma­chines and car­ries work­ing cap­i­tal. It needs re­li­able elec­tric­ity, it moves goods, and it pays back over five to seven years, not one or two.
## The cathe­dral

Last come con­tracts. Global buy­ers run just-in-time sup­ply. If a sup­plier fails to de­liver 5,000 ball bear­ings on the day, the as­sem­bly line freezes, and a court should promptly im­pose liq­ui­dated dam­ages. Without that, firms hoard in­ven­tory or deal only with fam­ily. {104-C05}
Nor is this low-skill work, Shah said. It is “a high wire act” of per­fect qual­ity, quan­tity and tim­ing. {104-C06}
~ Amit Varma’s shorter an­swer was that IT ser­vices were new, so no decades of reg­u­la­tion lay in wait for them. Manufacturing in­her­ited it all. {104-C02}

quote.text: to do man­u­fac­tur­ing well is to achieve a cathe­dral of com­plex­ity, where there’s a rich array of con­tracts that sur­round the process of man­u­fac­tur­ing

sections.label: How we got here
sections.head: Forgivable, then unforgivable
sections.caption: the state’s long war on factories
body: India’s fall to 2 per cent of world man­u­fac­tur­ing came under the British, Amit Varma said, and owed much to the Industrial Revolution. Independent India made things worse.

Jawaharlal Nehru made two big mis­takes. Import sub­sti­tu­tion cut India off[[x12]] from world trade, and its share fell from about 2 per cent in 1947 to 0.5 per cent by 1990. In the 1960s, Hong Kong’s in­come from ex­ports was as much as India’s en­tire in­come. {#hongkong}

The sec­ond was P.C. Mahalanobis’s be­lief that com­pe­ti­tion is waste­ful: why should two com­pa­nies make cars? So many ex­ist­ing laws still rest on it, Varma said. “Why should ten peo­ple make potato chips?” {104-J17}
## After 1965

Varma finds it hard to blame Nehru, who fol­lowed the fash­ion of the times. But by 1965 the model was vis­i­bly fail­ing. He called Indira Gandhi’s eco­nomic poli­cies crimes on hu­man­ity[[x13]]. {#indira}

The list is long: in­dus­trial li­cens­ing, the MRTP Act against big firms, small-scale reser­va­tions for goods such as gar­ments and shoes, FERA against for­eign cap­i­tal, and the Industrial Disputes Act, under which a firm of 100 work­ers needed state per­mis­sion to fire any­one. Firms stayed at 99, or 19, or nine. {104-C08}
~ The 1970s, when cheap labour could have made India a man­u­fac­tur­ing su­per­power, were lost. “We sim­ply never got on that bus,” Varma said.

quote.text: What hap­pened after 1965, frankly, is un­for­giv­able. We knew we were on the wrong track and we deep­ened our jour­ney into that wrong track.

sections.label: Today, part one
sections.head: Factories belong in cities
sections.caption: what holds factories back today
body: Ajay Shah listed twelve prob­lems that hold Indian man­u­fac­tur­ing back today. The first is labour.

Maharashtra, he granted, has reined in wild­cat unions. “I will point out that there are many states in India that are not called Maharashtra,” he added. {104-J07} Unions, he said, are a form of mar­ket power, which the state should coun­ter­act, not en­shrine.
Then min­i­mum wages. As Milton Friedman ex­plained[[x14]], Amit Varma said, a min­i­mum wage does not lift a low-paid worker to the legal floor: it out­laws his job. {104-R08}
Infrastructure has im­proved a great deal, Shah said, with­out a match­ing rise in FDI, man­u­fac­tur­ing ex­ports or fac­tory jobs, so it is no longer the bind­ing con­straint[[x15]]. {104-R09}
## Where the work­ers live

Land is the third prob­lem, and where work­ers will live the fourth. Prices, Shah said, look like a China-style bub­ble. A vil­lage of 150 house­holds has about 750 peo­ple, of whom at most 100 would go to one fac­tory. {#village} Factories be­long near cities, built into urban plan­ning.
Electricity comes next, then trade bar­ri­ers: a 10 per cent duty on the yarn for syn­thetic fab­ric makes Indian cloth dearer than Bangladesh’s or Vietnam’s. {104-C12}
~ Shah finds the Chinese dor­mi­tory model, in which fac­to­ries build hos­tels for work­ers, deeply dis­sat­is­fy­ing.

quote.text: So you should get out of the ro­man­tic idea that there will be fac­to­ries near vil­lages.

sections.label: Today, part two
sections.head: Pay up, scale up, fly out
sections.caption: finance, size, courts and taxes
body: Finance is the sev­enth prob­lem. Big Indian com­pa­nies rou­tinely squeeze small sup­pli­ers on pay­ments, which Ajay Shah calls short-sighted, since big firms have cheaper cap­i­tal. The an­swer is not a gov­ern­ment in­voice por­tal but a bank­ruptcy code that em­pow­ers op­er­a­tional cred­i­tors[[x17]]. Push ten im­por­tant big com­pa­nies into bank­ruptcy, he said, and ev­ery­one else will get the mes­sage. {104-C13}

The eighth prob­lem is the state’s view of the world. “The en­tire Indian state is or­gan­ised as an au­tarky,” Shah said. A tax of­fi­cer who finds a for­eign bank ac­count sus­pects hawala. {104-C17}
## Size and the courts

Ninth is size. By Wright’s Law[[x16]], each dou­bling of life­time out­put lifts pro­duc­tiv­ity by about 20 per cent, and in a fac­tory of 10,000 ma­chines every sub­tle op­ti­mi­sa­tion pays. India feels good about 2,000-worker plants; low-cost lead­ers else­where em­ploy 10,000 to 100,000. {104-C16}
Tenth come the courts. The hosts’ friend Shubho Roy ar­gues that if courts award only 5 per cent in­ter­est after ten years of stalling, the de­faulter has won a cheap loan. {104-C14}
Eleventh, ex­porters should get back all the in­di­rect tax they pay. Twelfth, firms must be able to hire for­eign tal­ent eas­ily.
~ Five of the twelve sit with the union gov­ern­ment, Shah said, and seven with the states. {104-C18}

quote.text: In a very big fac­tory, if you have ten thou­sand ma­chines, every sub­tle op­ti­mi­sa­tion is worth it.

art.caption: Ajay Shah on finance, size, courts and taxes

quote.text: The labour laws in India, which are os­ten­si­bly meant to pro­tect work­ers, ac­tu­ally hurt work­ers the more. It’s a clas­sic ex­am­ple of why you should judge a pol­icy not by its in­ten­tion, but by its out­come.

p3.title: Tales from the shop floor
p3.deck: Four stories the hosts told, from Baroda’s pipes to Infosys’s licence

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on India’s manufacturing before 1947
stories.head: From a quarter of the world to 2%
body: In 1750, Amit Varma said, India pro­duced about 20 to 25 per cent of the world’s man­u­fac­tur­ing out­put. There were no ma­chines yet; all of it was ar­ti­sanal. “We were doing damn well.” {#share1750}
By 1900, the share had fallen to about 2 per cent. Historians tell two sto­ries about why, Varma said, and there is some truth in both.

One ac­count, which Dadabhai Naoroji fa­mously gave in the British Parliament, blames colo­nial­ism: cheap ma­chine-made cot­ton tex­tiles from Manchester poured into India and de­stroyed its weavers. In that telling, Varma said, the British are com­pletely the vil­lains.

Other his­to­ri­ans, in­clud­ing Tirthankar Roy[[x18]], whom both hosts ad­mire, paint a dif­fer­ent pic­ture. The Industrial Revolution had ar­rived, and ar­ti­sans could not com­pete with fac­to­ries. Machine-spun fab­ric from England hurt hand­loom work­ers in places that were never colonised too.
“So it’s re­ally a shift in tech­nol­ogy, tech­no­log­i­cal ob­so­les­cence which is mak­ing this hap­pen,” Varma said. India was un­lucky to in­dus­tri­alise later. {104-S04}

Some in­dus­try did come. From the 1850s, some of it aided by British cap­i­tal, there were tex­tile mills in Bombay and Ahmedabad and jute mills in Bengal, and the Tata Iron and Steel Company was set up in 1907. Manufacturing’s share of out­put al­most dou­bled, from 3.8 per cent in 1913 to 7.5 per cent at Independence.
~ But out of about 350 mil­lion peo­ple, only two and a half mil­lion worked in man­u­fac­tur­ing. {#workers} That was the base the new coun­try in­her­ited.
stories.why: The vil­lain-only story leaves out tech­no­log­i­cal ob­so­les­cence, Varma ar­gued. India’s deeper mis­for­tune was to in­dus­tri­alise late, leav­ing a thin base that the in­de­pen­dent state then hob­bled fur­ther with li­cences, re­stric­tive laws and im­port sub­sti­tu­tion. {104-C07}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on India’s lost share of world manufacturing

stories.kicker: From Montek Singh Ahluwalia’s memoir, read by Amit Varma
stories.head: Licence granted, drive outdated
body: Amit Varma read an anec­dote from Montek Singh Ahluwalia’s mem­oir *Backstage*, told to Ahluwalia by Infosys’s co-founder Narayana Murthy. {104-S03}

In 1983, Infosys wanted to im­port a Data General MV 8000 com­puter[[x19]] with three re­mov­able disk drives of 200 MB each. Its peo­ple had to make sev­eral trips to New Delhi to get the im­port li­cence.

By the time the li­cence came, a new disk drive with a ca­pac­ity of 300 MB was avail­able, and it was 30 per cent cheaper. Naturally, they wanted the lat­est model. But the li­cence named the model num­ber, and sev­eral more vis­its to Delhi were needed to change it.
~ In an area where tech­nol­ogy was chang­ing rapidly and timely de­liv­ery of ex­port or­ders was cru­cial, Ahluwalia wrote, long de­lays in get­ting equip­ment were fatal for ex­porters.
stories.why: Where tech­nol­ogy changes faster than files move, li­cens­ing was not only mis­taken in prin­ci­ple but un­work­able in prac­tice. Under it, Varma said, the state de­ter­mined every ac­tion a pri­vate player took. {#licensing}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the Infosys import licence

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a chemical complex near Baroda
stories.head: Pipe dreams in Baroda
body: In the Baroda re­gion, Ajay Shah has seen an en­tire chem­i­cal in­dus­try com­plex[[x21]] in which sev­eral pri­vate fac­to­ries run pipes to one an­other. He called it one of the most mag­i­cal things he has seen. {104-S01}

The out­put of one fac­tory flows down a pipe into the next. A meter records how much has gone across, and the sup­plier in­voices on that basis. No trucks, no han­dling: “there is no fric­tion at all be­cause it’s flow­ing on pipes”.
This, Shah said, is what the econ­o­mist Albert Hirschman called link­ages[[x20]]: spe­cialised firms, phys­i­cally close, buy­ing from and sell­ing to one an­other.

~ In India such net­works are frag­ile. Imagine friends plan­ning twenty in­ter­linked fac­to­ries within 10 km of one an­other near Nashik, Shah said: some­thing trips up five out of the ten, and the link­ages never come to­gether. {104-C04}

quote.text: com­plex­ity doesn’t work well in India be­cause there are too many buggy com­po­nents in our Indian land­scape

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the pipes of Baroda

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the power supply where they recorded
stories.head: Lights out, 70 km from Bombay
body: The hosts recorded this episode in rural Maharashtra, a scant 70 km from Bombay. About ten times a day, Ajay Shah said, the MSEB power tripped[[x22]]. {104-S02}

For a man­u­fac­turer, that is a no-go: no fac­tory can have its equip­ment trip five or ten times a day. So ev­ery­body has to get a gen­er­a­tor, which bulks up cap­i­tal costs. And run­ning a fac­tory on diesel, Shah said, is hor­ren­dously ex­pen­sive.

Buying from the grid is no es­cape. Commercial and in­dus­trial users are over­charged so that the state can sub­sidise farm­ers who get free or nearly free power, house­holds who get 200 or 500 units free, and peo­ple who sim­ply steal it.
~ “All this stuff,” Shah said, “is loaded on the backs of the C and I.” Only Gujarat, he added, works rea­son­ably well. {104-C11}

quote.text: it’s as­ton­ish­ing how 10 times a day the MSEB power trips. Like what is this non­sense?

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 104. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Jawaharlal Nehru (Keystone View Company/FPG, public domain); Indira Gandhi (India, GODL-India); Milton Friedman (Bachrach Studios, public domain); Charlie Chaplin (Strauss-Peyton Studio, public domain). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon and Wikipedia.

shelf.title: How Frameworks (howframeworks.com)
shelf.creator: Sudhir Sarnobat
shelf.why: It of­fers frame­works to grow a busi­ness, turn it around or take it to the next level.

shelf.title: India’s MSME Landscape — Some Useful Frameworks (Episode 419, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Sudhir Sarnobat and Naren Shenoy
shelf.why: Ajay calls it one of the best Seen and the Unseen episodes he has ex­pe­ri­enced.

shelf.title: Modern Times
shelf.creator: Charlie Chaplin
shelf.why: The film cap­tures the men­tal image most peo­ple carry when they hear ‘eco­nomic development’.

shelf.title: Why Freedom Matters (Episode 10, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Despite the title, an eco­nomic his­tory of India told through the lens of free­dom: the boom after 1869, Nehru’s Fabian so­cial­ism, the lost years from the 1962 war to the Emergency, and the open­ing-up that lifted mil­lions out of poverty.

shelf.title: The History of the Planning Commission (Episode 306, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: It goes into de­tail on the Mahalanobis pe­riod and the plan­ning mind­set that held that com­pe­ti­tion is waste­ful.

shelf.title: Backstage
shelf.creator: Montek Singh Ahluwalia
shelf.why: Montek Singh Ahluwalia’s mem­oir of the re­form years, full of human de­tail about work­ing in­side the sys­tem and con­crete ex­am­ples of how li­cens­ing stran­gled Indian en­ter­prise.

shelf.title: The Life and Times of Montek Singh Ahluwalia (Episode 285, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Montek Singh Ahluwalia
shelf.why: Montek Singh Ahluwalia’s first-hand ac­count of his decades in the re­form en­gine room and the ‘silent revolution’ that built up from the late 1970s.

shelf.title: Milton Friedman on the minimum wage
shelf.creator: Milton Friedman
shelf.why: Friedman’s short video ar­gu­ment that a min­i­mum wage doesn’t lift a low-productivity worker’s pay to the legal floor: it makes the job il­le­gal, so the wage drops to zero.

shelf.title: Where Has All the Infrastructure Gone? (Episode 55, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: A first-principles chal­lenge to India’s op­ti­mism about every new road and air­port: in­fra­struc­ture has di­min­ish­ing re­turns, and big re­cent gains brought no com­pa­ra­ble rise in FDI, man­u­fac­tur­ing ex­ports or jobs.

shelf.title: The Lowest Hanging Fruit on the Coconut Tree
shelf.creator: Akshay Jaitly and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Akshay Jaitly and Ajay’s case for a mar­ket-based elec­tric­ity sec­tor that drives India’s cli­mate tran­si­tion through the price sys­tem, rather than the state pick­ing favoured tech­nolo­gies.

shelf.title: Climate Change and Our Power Sector (Episode 278, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Akshay Jaitly and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Akshay Jaitly and Ajay on cli­mate change and India’s power sec­tor, cen­tred on the elec­tric­ity grid: the con­ver­sa­tional ver­sion of their case for re­form­ing elec­tric­ity.

shelf.title: The Brave New Future of Electricity (Episode 40, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s mas­ter­class on the power sec­tor: solar, wind, stor­age and time-of-day pric­ing, why elec­tric­ity prices must be al­lowed to move, and why fix­ing Indian power is a 25-year jour­ney that Indian man­u­fac­tur­ing de­pends on.

shelf.title: The Globalisation Episode (Episode 95, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ foun­da­tional think­ing on glob­al­i­sa­tion: first prin­ci­ples, a pot­ted in­tel­lec­tual his­tory up to the Second World War, and why tar­iffs harm a country’s own peo­ple and shift wealth from the poor to the rich.

shelf.title: Is Globalization Doomed? (Episode 96, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The sec­ond part of the glob­al­i­sa­tion two-parter: how the open in­ter­na­tional order broke down, mainly be­cause China, and to a lesser ex­tent India, didn’t play by the rules, and why trade bar­ri­ers crip­ple man­u­fac­tur­ing.

shelf.title: Going Bankrupt in India (Episode 80, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why bank­ruptcy is a healthy, nor­mal part of eco­nomic life, and how the pol­i­tics of India’s bank­ruptcy re­form gave big com­pa­nies out­sized in­flu­ence, left op­er­a­tional cred­i­tors weak and squeezed small manufacturers’ work­ing cap­i­tal.

shelf.title: The Beauty of Finance (Episode 21, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s mas­ter­class on why fi­nance ex­ists and why it mat­ters to the real econ­omy: fi­nance as ‘the brain of the economy’, not a casino for the rich, traced back to me­dieval trad­ing voy­ages.

shelf.title: The Journey of Indian Finance (Episode 71, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: An insider’s ac­count of how Indian fi­nance was built: 25 years in which the fi­nance min­istry, SEBI, NSE and aca­demics worked to­gether, and how re­form pe­tered out once that group scat­tered.

shelf.title: The Journey of Indian Finance
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s eco­nomic his­tory of Indian fi­nance from 1947 to today, which Amit calls close to mag­is­te­rial and the de­fin­i­tive work on the sub­ject.

shelf.title: The Power of Moore’s Laws (Episode 87, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Built around Wright’s Law: pro­duc­tiv­ity rises about 20% with each dou­bling of cu­mu­la­tive out­put, so vol­ume drives down costs and tiny fac­to­ries can’t com­pete, in ser­vices as well as man­u­fac­tur­ing.

shelf.title: New work on district courts in Kerala
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: He sees it as the first time India is get­ting se­ri­ous process im­prove­ments in the ju­di­ciary.

shelf.title: Bimal Patel’s talk at the Emerging Markets Conference
shelf.creator: Bimal Patel
shelf.why: Patel lays out one uni­fy­ing theme for urban plan­ning: around 40% of land should go to streets and parks, with a mech­a­nism for money to flow back into urban in­fra­struc­ture.

laughs.text: Amit on Ajay prais­ing his MSME episode: it’s like a novice song­writer tak­ing his song to Bob Dylan and Dylan say­ing ‘Wow, this is such a great song.’ For Amit to do a man­u­fac­tur­ing episode and have Ajay call it good ‘is ex­actly the same thing.’

Before record­ing, while going through point­ers on in­dus­trial pol­icy and labour laws, Ajay de­clared he was hav­ing so much fun. Amit: ‘Bhai, you are hav­ing fun. I’m try­ing to mem­o­rize phrases, you are hav­ing fun.’
Ajay boasts that ser­vices ex­ports grew 126% in a decade, ‘noth­ing to sneeze at’. Amit: ‘That hap­pened to my weight, but con­tinue.’

Ajay adapts Shakespeare’s Julius Caesar to de­scribe Indian sup­ply chains: ‘Then burst his mighty heart, and muf­fling up his face, even at the base of Pompey’s statue, great Caesar fell… Ingratitude more strong than traitors’ arms van­quished him. No, I want to say in­com­pe­tence more strong than traitors’ arms van­quished him.’

Ajay’s ‘North Korea-South Korea comparison’: ‘a com­mu­nist coun­try called West Bengal, where the min­i­mum wage is 13,000 ru­pees, and a cap­i­tal­ist coun­try called East Bengal’ with a min­i­mum wage of 7,000-8,000. Guess which one built the suc­cess­ful gar­ment ex­port in­dus­try.
Ajay grants that Maharashtra has reined in wild­cat unions, then adds: ‘I will point out that there are many states in India that are not called Maharashtra.’
Ajay says a 2,000-worker fac­tory ‘ain’t much’ glob­ally. Amit jokes: ‘Some would dream of a fac­tory with 1.7 bil­lion peo­ple… Manufacturing na­tional pride.’
Amit on the Nehru era: the world didn’t yet know the Soviet Union was ‘a com­plete and utter fail­ure. It was re­ally a pub­lic re­la­tions suc­cess.’
Amit after Ajay’s twelve-point di­ag­no­sis: ‘I will watch this episode again and again and again and maybe get our ed­i­tor to do a ver­sion of it that doesn’t have me and only you.’
James C. Scott’s idea of ‘legibility’ from Seeing Like a State, used to ex­plain why vis­i­ble fac­to­ries at­tract ex­tor­tion from goons and in­spec­tors.
Albert Hirschman’s ‘linkages’: the net­work ef­fects cre­ated when spe­cialised fac­to­ries buy from and sell to each other.
Adam Smith’s pin fac­tory, cited for the prin­ci­ple that each fac­tory should do one thing well in­stead of one cam­pus doing twenty things badly.

P.C. Mahalanobis’s mid-1950s claim that com­pe­ti­tion is waste­ful (‘Why should two com­pa­nies make cars, one is enough’). Amit notes it still un­der­lies laws today: ‘Why should ten peo­ple make potato chips?’
